headline: TSMC beat and raised its 2026 growth outlook to about 44%, but the AI selloff went global anyway: the KOSPI fell 7.6%, the Nikkei about 5%, Oracle's default insurance hit a record, and September producer prices jumped 1.3%.
summary: TSMC answered yesterday's question on the numbers: Q3 revenue was $46.72 billion, up 41.2%, gross margin 66.4% sat inside the 65% to 67% guide, Q4 is guided to $52.3 to $54.3 billion, and 2026 growth was raised to about 44% with capex held at $60 to $64 billion. The stock still fell about 2% in Taipei and about 1.9% in New York premarket, because the market is now selling AI on rates and debt, not on demand. On Oct 14 the Nasdaq fell 1.88% to 26,692.87 and the S&P 500 1.11% to 7,718.94, CoreWeave dropped about 15% as its bonds traded near 15% yields, and Oracle's five year default insurance hit a record 288 basis points. Overnight the KOSPI fell 7.57% into a bear market and the Nikkei about 4.9%, with Advantest down about 15%. This morning September producer prices rose 1.3% in the month and 6.3% from a year ago, the biggest monthly jump since March 2022, yet the 10 year yield fell to about 5.10% as money moved from tech into bonds, health care and energy. The dashboard's prices are still Oct 13 closes, so treat every setup and verdict below as one day old.

regime.why: Risk off in AI hardware, memory and Asia; risk on in energy and health care, which led on Oct 14. Bond yields fell even after a hot producer price report, which says investors are buying safety, not betting on growth. Normal size only on breakouts that close over the pivot on 1.5x volume, and no new chip or memory swings until the selling stops.

signals.title: TSMC passes the test on paper: record quarter, 66.4% margin inside the guide, 2026 growth raised to about 44%, but the stock falls with the rest of AI
signals.since_yesterday: TSMC reported on Oct 15: Q3 revenue $46.72 billion, gross margin 66.4%, Q4 guide $52.3 to $54.3 billion, 2026 growth raised to about 44%, capex unchanged at $60 to $64 billion.
signals.what_happened: TSMC's Q3 revenue was NT$1,494.24 billion, or $46.72 billion, up 41.2% in dollars and above its own guidance. Net income was a record NT$763.06 billion, up 68.7%, or $4.60 per ADR against about $4.42 expected. Gross margin was 66.4%, inside the 65% to 67% guide but down 1.3 points from Q2 because the 2 nm ramp dilutes margins; operating margin was 58.7%. Q4 is guided to $52.3 to $54.3 billion, about 14% more than Q3 and 58% more than a year ago, with a 65% to 67% gross margin. TSMC raised 2026 growth to about 44% in dollars from slightly above 40% and kept 2026 capex at $60 to $64 billion; Q3 capex was $13.8 billion. It gave no 2027 capex number, only that 2026 to 2028 spending will be well above the prior three years. CEO C.C. Wei said AI demand is 'extremely robust and far above our supply capability', but management said it is planning 2027 prudently for consumer and price sensitive markets. Shares fell about 2% in Taipei and the ADR was down about 1.9% premarket from an Oct 14 close of about $430.
signals.so_what: Yesterday we said the risk was weak margins or a capex cut. Neither happened, and that matters: the AI chokepoint is still sold out. So today's chip selling is about the price of money and the debt behind the build out, not about demand. Who gets paid: TSMC and the tool makers it buys from, because 2026 to 2028 spending stays high. Who is exposed: the companies borrowing to buy the chips (see the credit signal). Second order: if demand is real but buyers' financing gets expensive, the weakest buyers slow first, and the strongest (Microsoft, Google, Meta) gain share. What would make this wrong: a big customer cuts orders, or TSMC trims 2027 plans in January.
signals.for_you: Swing: the 'wait for TSMC' rule is done, and the answer is still wait. ANET left the swing setups (its Oct 13 close was 204.52 against a 217.85 pivot) and chips fell again Oct 14 and premarket Oct 15. Long term: TSM has no buy zone verdict (Not enough data). LRCX slipped to 'Buy zone, wait for the chart' (up/down volume 0.96, needs 1.0 or more). ANET turned 'Buy zone now' on Oct 13 data (204.52, top of a 156.98 to 204.84 zone), but that was before the Oct 14 and 15 selloff, so wait for the next refresh before a first tranche.

signals.title: The AI unwind goes global: KOSPI falls 7.57% into a bear market, Nikkei about 4.9%, Advantest about 15%, Micron down another 4.1%
signals.since_yesterday: The KOSPI fell 7.57% to 5,554.22 on Oct 15 and tripped a circuit breaker; the Nikkei fell about 4.9% and Taiwan saw record foreign selling.
signals.what_happened: South Korea's KOSPI closed down 7.57% at 5,554.22 on Oct 15, its seventh straight loss and lowest close since April 7; a sell side sidecar hit at 9:07am and a Level 1 circuit breaker at 12:38pm. Korea Times puts the index about 40% below its June 19 peak of 9,385. SK hynix fell about 11% to 1,262,000 won and Samsung Electronics about 9.5% to 210,000 won. Japan's Nikkei fell 4.9% to 64,425.95 (Japan Times), with Advantest down about 15% and SoftBank Group down 8% to 10%. Taiwan's Taiex had its sixth biggest daily point loss with a record net foreign sale of NT$302.56 billion (Focus Taiwan); the close was not confirmed, about 3.4% lower per AP. In the US, Micron closed Oct 14 at $914.13, down 4.1%, and was down about 4% premarket Oct 15. Analysts blamed doubts about returns on AI spending, a possible glut from China's CXMT, and the risk of another Fed hike. Server DRAM spot prices are still rising, per MoneyToday.
signals.so_what: This is a positioning unwind: Korea and Japan were the most crowded AI trades and foreigners are leaving all at once. Rising spot DRAM prices say the memory shortage is not over yet, so the stocks are falling faster than the business. Who pays: anyone in memory and chip testing (SK hynix, Samsung, Micron, Advantest). Who gets paid: buyers of memory if prices ever fall, and, later, patient long term buyers. What would make this wrong: a Fed hike on Oct 28 or a failed SK hynix report on Oct 28 would mean the selling has further to run.
signals.for_you: No action. No memory or chip test swings: no setup qualifies and the trend is down. If you sell puts, do not sell them on MU, chip testers or EWY into a falling market just because premiums are rich. Watch SK hynix (Oct 28) and Samsung (Oct 29) earnings; MU has no dashboard verdict (Not enough data).

signals.title: AI credit stress: Oracle's default insurance hits a record 288 basis points and CoreWeave's bonds trade near 15% yields
signals.what_happened: CoreWeave fell about 15% on Oct 14 after its bond yields jumped: its 9.625% notes due 2032 yielded about 14.8% and its 2031 notes about 14.9%, levels that credit markets usually reserve for distressed borrowers; it was down another 4.5% to 6.3% premarket Oct 15. CEO Mike Intrator called the reaction irrational. Oracle's five year credit default swaps widened 26 basis points to a record 288 (S&P Global data via Reuters), and CDS spreads for Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia also hit record wide levels, though far below Oracle's. Reuters said CoreWeave, Oracle and other AI names erased about $80 billion of market value on Oct 14, and Nvidia closed down 3.16% at $221.30. Background: on Sep 24 Oracle sent a force majeure notice on its Project Jupiter campus in New Mexico, which still lacks a gas pipeline and permits for its power plant; Bloomberg reported the $18 billion construction loan trades below 90 cents on the dollar.
signals.so_what: Follow the money backwards: the AI build out is now partly paid for with borrowed money, and lenders are asking for more to take the risk. When the cost of debt rises, the weakest borrowers (neoclouds like CoreWeave, and Oracle, which leans on debt) slow first. Who pays: their shareholders and bondholders, and the chip and power suppliers that counted on their orders. Who gets paid: cash rich buyers (Microsoft, Google, Meta) who can keep building without borrowing, and lenders who can now charge more. Third order: TSMC says demand is far above supply, so if a weak buyer cancels, a strong one may take the slot; the risk is to the borrowers more than to the chokepoint. What would make this wrong: yields keep falling and CoreWeave refinances smoothly.
signals.for_you: Long term: no change to buy zones from this alone, but it argues for owning the cash rich names and the chokepoints, not the borrowers. CRWV is on the scorecard as a long term call from Oct 6 (down 15.03% against SPY after 5 days); ORCL was a long term call from Oct 7 that lagged SPY by 6.22 points. Puts: avoid selling puts on heavily indebted AI names; a falling bond price usually comes before more stock weakness. Swing: none.

signals.title: Inflation day two: September producer prices jump 1.3%, the most since March 2022, yet the 10 year falls to about 5.10% as money leaves tech
signals.since_yesterday: PPI rose 1.3% in September and 6.3% from a year ago (released Oct 15), and the 10 year yield fell to about 5.10% instead of rising.
signals.what_happened: The producer price index rose 1.3% in September and 6.3% from a year earlier, against forecasts of about 0.5% to 0.6% and 5.3% to 5.5%; it was the biggest monthly jump since March 2022 and the highest yearly rate since December 2022, driven largely by energy (CNN, BLS). The core measure without food, energy and trade rose 0.5% in the month and 5.0% from a year ago (CNBC). On Oct 14 the S&P 500 closed down 1.11% at 7,718.94, the Nasdaq down 1.88% at 26,692.87, the Dow down 0.09% at 51,621.48 and the Russell 2000 down 1.93%; technology was the worst sector, down 3.00%. The 10 year yield ended Oct 14 at 5.19%, about 2 basis points lower after an early jump, and was about 5.099% on Oct 15 morning. Fed officials split: New York Fed President Williams said one more hike this year is appropriate but sees none in 2027; Chicago's Goolsbee wants more data; San Francisco's Daly said more hikes are likely but not urgent. CME FedWatch odds of an Oct 28 hike rose to about 35% from 22.1% after CPI. September retail sales and weekly jobless claims were also due at 8:30am ET; their results were not found at writing.
signals.so_what: Two hot inflation prints in two days, and yields fell. That is the bond market saying it fears a growth or credit accident more than inflation, at least today. Who pays: companies that must pass on higher input costs (producer prices lead consumer prices by a few months), and long duration growth stocks. Who gets paid: energy producers now, and bond holders if the flight to safety continues. Second order: if the Fed hikes on Oct 28 into a tech and credit selloff, the risk of a policy mistake rises. What would make this wrong: October energy prices fall back and core producer prices cool.
signals.for_you: Swing: favor energy and health care setups that confirm on volume; skip tech breakouts this week. Puts: richer premiums, but only on names you want to own through a 20% drop; see Setups for live quotes. Long term: buy in small tranches only where the verdict is 'Buy zone now' and the chart still holds after the next refresh.

signals.title: Oil: Ukraine ends the refinery pause and hits Ryazan, the US weighs easing shadow fleet sanctions, and COP closes over its pivot
signals.since_yesterday: Zelenskyy said Ukraine will resume refinery strikes and Russia reported a hit on the Ryazan refinery on Oct 15; the US is weighing easing shadow fleet sanctions; COP closed over its pivot on Oct 14.
signals.what_happened: Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian refineries after Russia kept hitting Ukraine's grid during the three day 'energy ceasefire'; on Oct 15 Russia said a Ukrainian drone started a fire at the Ryazan refinery, about 300 km southeast of Moscow (CNBC, Al Jazeera). Reuters reported Oct 14 that the US is weighing letting sanctioned 'shadow fleet' tankers carry oil that is not itself sanctioned, to cut record freight rates; analysts expect only a few extra ships. A Houthi spokesman said Oct 14 that attacks on Saudi oil sites and airports will continue (House of Saud citing Reuters and gCaptain; less established source). Brent was about $104.44 on Oct 15 morning, down about 1.5%. On Oct 14 Exxon closed at $177.01 (+1.68%) after a record intraday high, ConocoPhillips at $142.34 (+1.02%), and Chevron was quoted at $222.04 (+1.98%).
signals.so_what: Two forces pull oil in opposite ways: more Russian refinery damage tightens diesel, while the White House is trying hard to lower fuel prices before the Nov 3 midterms. Today the policy side won, with Brent down about 1.5%. Who gets paid: US producers with no Gulf or Russia exposure, at record highs. Who pays: airlines and truckers. Third order: a broken energy truce makes a Russia Ukraine deal less likely, which keeps a risk premium in diesel through winter.
signals.for_you: Swing: COP closed at 142.34 on Oct 14, over its 141.91 pivot, but the volume is not in the dashboard yet (needs 10M+ shares; up/down 1.22, 23.9% ahead of SPY over 3 months). Treat it as 'weak, wait' until Setups shows the Oct 14 volume. CVX's quote of 222.04 is over its 219.24 pivot, but the close and volume are unconfirmed (needs 12.8M+) and it reports Oct 30, so the window is short. XOM has left the setups after running from its base; its Oct 6 scorecard swing is open at +0.58R. Puts: no energy put idea.

cycle.short_term_debt_cycle: Late, and the first credit cracks are showing. The Fed is at 3.75% to 4.00% with hike odds near 35% for Oct 28, but the 10 year fell to about 5.10% from 5.19% as investors bought bonds for safety. Credit spreads are widening first in the most indebted AI borrowers: Oracle's CDS at a record 288 basis points and CoreWeave's bonds near 15%. In Dalio's terms, late in the short term cycle the tightening bites the weakest borrowers first.
cycle.long_term_debt_cycle: Late. Government debt is high, long rates are above 5%, and a growing share of the AI build out is financed with debt (Oracle's Jupiter campus loan trades below 90 cents). With inflation rising the Fed has little room to ease if credit breaks, which is the squeeze of a late long term cycle.
cycle.big_cycle: Four of the five forces are active. Debt and money: hot CPI and PPI, and widening AI credit spreads. Internal order: the White House is pushing to lower fuel prices before the Nov 3 midterms. External order: Ukraine resumed refinery strikes after the energy truce failed, and the Houthis vow more attacks on Saudi oil. Technology: TSMC says AI demand is far above supply, the main tailwind, now meeting the cost of money.
tailwinds: TSMC: AI demand 'far above' supply; 2026 growth raised to about 44% and Q4 guided up about 58% from a year ago.
Bond yields fell (10 year about 5.10%), which eases pressure on valuations if it lasts.
Health care and energy are absorbing money that leaves tech, so the broad market is falling less than the Nasdaq.
headwinds: Producer prices up 6.3% from a year ago, which feeds future consumer inflation.
Credit stress in AI borrowers: Oracle CDS at a record, CoreWeave bonds near 15%.
A global positioning unwind in chips: KOSPI -7.57%, Nikkei about -4.9% on Oct 15.

history.what: Telecom companies raised about $1.6 trillion, including about $600 billion of bonds, to build fiber networks on forecasts that traffic doubled every 100 days; it actually doubled about yearly. By late 2002 about 23 telecom companies had gone bankrupt.
history.lesson: In a debt funded build out, demand can be real and the borrowers can still fail if capacity runs ahead of revenue. The chokepoint suppliers with cash survived; the leveraged builders did not.

source.title: AI debt bubble: dot com and telecom lessons (IBTimes)

history.what: The Nasdaq fell 33.1% for the year while the Dow fell about 8.8% and the S&P 500 19.4%, the worst year since 2008.
history.lesson: When inflation forces rates up, money leaves long duration tech for steadier businesses; the spread between the Nasdaq and the Dow can be huge.

source.title: Stocks fall to end Wall Street's worst year since 2008 (NBC News, Dec 30, 2022)

cycle.differences: The telecom bust replaces the 1973 oil shock today because the new stress is debt behind the AI build out, not oil. What is different: the biggest AI buyers fund most spending from operating cash flow, unlike the fiber builders, and TSMC says demand still outruns supply, while in 2001 there was a glut. What rhymes: the marginal, debt funded builders (CoreWeave, Oracle's project finance) are where stress shows first, just as it did with Global Crossing and Metromedia Fiber.
cycle.for_you: Swing: trade only what confirms on volume, which today means energy or health care, not chips. Puts: sell only on cash rich names in the buy zone, and skip indebted AI names even if premiums look rich. Long term: favor chokepoints and cash rich buyers over borrowers, and add in small tranches.

principle.text: He who lives by the crystal ball will eat shattered glass.
principle.applied: Yesterday the plan was 'wait for TSMC'. TSMC beat on every line and the stock still fell, because the market moved on to rates and debt. No forecast of the report would have helped; position size and waiting for volume did.
